topic: Public Administration — Meaning, Nature, Scope & Evolution

items.title: Meaning, Nature & Scope of Public Administration
items.body:
## Meaning

- **Public Administration** = the management of public affairs — the machinery and processes by which government **implements law and public policy** to serve the people.
- Classic definitions: **L.D. White** — 'all operations having for their purpose the fulfilment or enforcement of public policy'; **Woodrow Wilson** — 'administration is the most obvious part of government; it is government in action; it is the executive, the operative, the most visible side of government'.

## Nature — two views

| View | Champions | What it covers |
|---|---|---|
| **Integral view** | Henri Fayol, L.D. White | ALL activities (managerial, clerical, technical, manual) to achieve public purposes |
| **Managerial view** | L. Gulick, W.F. Willoughby | ONLY the managerial functions of top officials — captured by **POSDCORB** |

## Scope

- **POSDCORB view (by process):** Planning, Organising, Staffing, Directing, Co-ordinating, Reporting, Budgeting.
- **Subject-matter view (by function):** defence, revenue, law & order, health, education, welfare, etc.
- **As a discipline**, Public Administration is both an **art** (practice of getting things done) and a developing **science/social science** (systematic study of organisation and management).
- **Public vs Private administration:** public administration operates under **political direction, rule of law, public accountability, the profit-is-not-the-goal principle and public scrutiny**, unlike private management.
keyPoints: Public Administration = the machinery/process by which government implements law and public policy.
Integral view (Fayol, L.D. White) = all activities; Managerial view (Gulick, Willoughby) = only POSDCORB-type management functions.
POSDCORB = Planning, Organising, Staffing, Directing, Co-ordinating, Reporting, Budgeting.
Scope mapped two ways: by process (POSDCORB) and by subject-matter (defence, revenue, welfare...).
Public administration differs from private by political direction, rule of law, public accountability and non-profit purpose.
items.mnemonic: POSDCORB order: 'Please Own Some Data Cause Reports Balance'.
items.source: Standard texts on Public Administration (Wilson 1887; L.D. White; Gulick & Urwick 1937)

items.title: Evolution of Public Administration as a Discipline
items.body:
## From Wilson to Good Governance

- **1887 — Woodrow Wilson**, 'The Study of Administration' (Political Science Quarterly): first plea to study administration as a **distinct discipline**; father of Public Administration.
- **Politics-Administration dichotomy** — Wilson and **Frank Goodnow** ('Politics and Administration', 1900) held **politics = expression of the state's will (policy)**, **administration = execution of that will**. Later criticised as unrealistic — administrators also shape policy.
- **Scientific Management** — F.W. Taylor (efficiency, one best way); influenced early administrative theory.
- **1937 — POSDCORB** — **Luther Gulick & Lyndall Urwick**, 'Papers on the Science of Administration'; the high-water mark of the 'principles' approach.
- **Max Weber — bureaucracy:** the **rational-legal** 'ideal-type' — hierarchy, division of labour, written rules, files, impersonality and merit-based career officials.

## The behavioural & post-behavioural turn

- **Human Relations** (Elton Mayo, Hawthorne studies), Herbert Simon's critique of 'proverbs of administration' (fact-value; bounded rationality).
- **New Public Administration (NPA)** — **Minnowbrook Conference I, 1968** (Dwight Waldo); Frank Marini (1971): stress on **social equity, relevance, values and change**.
- **New Public Management (NPM)** — 1980s-90s; **Christopher Hood (1991)**; **Osborne & Gaebler, 'Reinventing Government' (1992)**: market/managerial reforms, 'steering not rowing', citizen-as-customer.
- **New Public Service (NPS)** — **Robert & Janet Denhardt (2000/2003)**: 'serving, not steering'; democratic citizenship and public interest.
- **Good Governance** — the current paradigm: participation, rule of law, transparency, accountability, responsiveness, equity, effectiveness (UNESCAP eight attributes).
keyPoints: Woodrow Wilson (1887) founded the discipline; politics-administration dichotomy refined by Frank Goodnow (1900).
POSDCORB (Gulick & Urwick, 1937) marked the 'principles of administration' era.
Weber's ideal-type bureaucracy rests on rational-legal authority (hierarchy, rules, impersonality, merit).
New Public Administration (Minnowbrook, 1968) added social equity as a core value.
NPM (Hood 1991; Osborne-Gaebler 1992) = market managerialism, 'steering not rowing'; New Public Service (Denhardt) = 'serving not steering'.
The good-governance paradigm stresses participation, transparency, accountability and responsiveness.
items.source: Wilson (1887); Goodnow (1900); Gulick & Urwick (1937); Weber; Minnowbrook I (1968); Hood (1991); Osborne & Gaebler (1992); Denhardt & Denhardt (2003)

items.title: Administrative Ideas in Kautilya's Arthashastra
items.body:
## The first Indian treatise on statecraft

- The **Arthashastra**, by **Kautilya (Chanakya / Vishnugupta)**, mentor of Chandragupta Maurya, is India's earliest systematic work on **administration, economy and statecraft** (in Sanskrit; 15 books, 180 chapters).

## Saptanga — the seven limbs of the state

| Element (Prakriti) | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Swami** | The king (sovereign) |
| **Amatya** | Ministers & civil servants |
| **Janapada** | Territory & people |
| **Durga** | Fort |
| **Kosha** | Treasury |
| **Danda / Bala** | Army / force |
| **Mitra** | Ally |

## Administrative organisation

- **Mantriparishad** — council of ministers advising the king (advice not binding).
- **Amatyas / Mantrins** — the higher civil service, chosen for merit and character.
- **Adhyakshas** — a large body of **superintendents** heading departments (mines, agriculture, trade, weights, etc.).
- **Espionage** — an elaborate intelligence network of spies (**gudhapurushas**) to check officials and gauge public opinion.
- **Yogakshema** — the king's cardinal duty to promote the **welfare and security** of subjects ('in the happiness of his subjects lies the king's happiness').
- Detailed norms on **taxation, salaries, audit, punishment (Danda-niti) and anti-corruption** — Kautilya famously warned that just as one cannot tell when a fish drinks water, one cannot tell when an official misappropriates revenue.
keyPoints: Arthashastra by Kautilya (Chanakya/Vishnugupta) = India's earliest systematic treatise on administration and statecraft.
Saptanga theory = seven limbs: Swami, Amatya, Janapada, Durga, Kosha, Danda, Mitra.
Mantriparishad = council of ministers; Amatyas/Mantrins = higher civil servants chosen on merit.
Adhyakshas = departmental superintendents; a vast espionage network (gudhapurushas) checked officials.
Yogakshema = the king's duty to ensure subjects' welfare and security; detailed anti-corruption and audit norms.
items.mnemonic: Saptanga: 'Swami And Janata Deserve Kosha, Danda, Mitra' (S-A-J-D-K-D-M).
items.source: Kautilya's Arthashastra (Saptanga theory; administrative organisation; Yogakshema)

items.title: Mughal Administration
items.body:
## A centralised, bureaucratic monarchy

- The Mughals (esp. **Akbar**) built a **centralised administration** with the emperor at the apex, assisted by great officers of state.

### Central officers

| Office | Charge |
|---|---|
| **Wazir / Diwan** | Revenue & finance |
| **Mir Bakshi** | Military pay, mansabdari, intelligence |
| **Khan-i-Saman** | Royal household & karkhanas |
| **Sadr-us-Sudur** | Religious affairs, grants & charity |
| **Qazi-ul-Quzat** | Chief judge (justice) |

## Mansabdari system (introduced by Akbar)

- Every officer held a **mansab (rank)** with two numbers: **Zat** (personal status/rank and pay) and **Sawar** (number of **cavalry/horsemen** to maintain).
- Mansabdars were **paid in cash or by jagir** (revenue assignment); the system was **non-hereditary** and transferable — a check on the nobility.

## Land revenue — Todar Mal's Dahsala (Zabti)

- Raja **Todar Mal's Zabti / Dahsala system (c. 1580)** fixed revenue on a **ten-year average** of yields and prices, standardising measurement and assessment.
- Revenue was the state's chief income; other systems (Kankut, Batai/Ghalla-Bakshi, Nasaq) also existed.

## Provincial hierarchy

- **Subah** (province, under a **Subedar/Nazim**) → **Sarkar** (district, **Faujdar** for law & order) → **Pargana** (**Shiqdar**; **Amil/Amalguzar** for revenue) → **Village** (Muqaddam, Patwari).
- Akbar organised the empire into **15 Subahs** (later expanded to about 20).
keyPoints: Central officers: Wazir/Diwan (revenue), Mir Bakshi (military/mansabdari), Khan-i-Saman (household), Sadr-us-Sudur (religious), Qazi (justice).
Mansabdari (Akbar): Zat = personal rank/pay, Sawar = cavalry to be maintained; non-hereditary, paid in cash or jagir.
Todar Mal's Zabti/Dahsala system (c.1580) assessed revenue on a ten-year average of yields and prices.
Provincial hierarchy: Subah (Subedar) > Sarkar (Faujdar) > Pargana (Shiqdar/Amil) > Village.
Akbar divided the empire into 15 Subahs (later ~20).
items.source: Standard accounts of Mughal administration (Ain-i-Akbari; Mansabdari; Todar Mal's Dahsala)

items.title: Legacy of British Rule — Charter Acts, ICS & Portfolio System
items.body:
## Evolution of the civil service through the Charter Acts

| Act | Administrative significance |
|---|---|
| **Charter Act 1793** | Cornwallis organised the **covenanted civil service**; recruitment by Company patronage |
| **Charter Act 1813** | Renewed charter; allowed missionaries; Company monopoly ended (except tea & China trade) |
| **Charter Act 1833** | Created the post of **Governor-General of India** (Bentinck); Macaulay proposed open competition (not implemented) |
| **Charter Act 1853** | Introduced **open competitive examination** for the civil service, ending patronage |

## The Indian Civil Service (ICS)

- **Cornwallis** is called the **'father of the civil service in India'** — he professionalised it, raised salaries and barred private trade.
- The first competitive exam was held in **London (1855)**; **Satyendranath Tagore** was the **first Indian in the ICS (1863)**.
- The **Aitchison Committee (1886)** and later reforms Indianised recruitment; exams began to be held in India (Allahabad, 1922).
- The ICS was called the **'steel frame' of India** (Lloyd George, 1922) — the durable core of the administrative state.

## The portfolio system & other legacies

- **Lord Canning** introduced the **portfolio system**, formalised by the **Indian Councils Act, 1861** — distributing government business among individual council members (forerunner of the cabinet system).
- Enduring British legacies: **rule of law, an independent-style permanent civil service, all-India services, the secretariat system, the district Collector, a codified legal system, budgeting and audit (CAG), and local self-government (Ripon, 1882).**
keyPoints: Charter Act 1793 (Cornwallis) organised the covenanted civil service; 1853 introduced open competition, ending patronage.
Charter Act 1833 created the Governor-General of India; Macaulay's competition proposal was not then implemented.
Cornwallis = 'father of the civil service in India'; first ICS exam London 1855; Satyendranath Tagore first Indian (1863).
ICS was dubbed the 'steel frame' of India (Lloyd George, 1922).
Portfolio system introduced by Lord Canning, formalised by the Indian Councils Act 1861.
British legacies: rule of law, permanent civil service, all-India services, secretariat, district Collector, CAG audit, local self-government.
items.source: Charter Acts 1793-1853; Indian Councils Act 1861; history of the Indian Civil Service

items.title: Civil Services, Reforms & the AP Administrative Structure
items.body:
## Civil services in India — constitutional basis

- **Part XIV of the Constitution (Articles 308-323)** — 'Services under the Union and the States'.
  - **Art 309** — recruitment & conditions of service.
  - **Art 310** — **doctrine of pleasure** (services hold office during the pleasure of the President/Governor).
  - **Art 311** — **safeguards** against arbitrary dismissal, removal or reduction in rank.
  - **Art 312** — Parliament may create a **new All India Service** only on a **Rajya Sabha resolution passed by two-thirds** of members present and voting.
- **Three All India Services:** IAS, IPS and the **Indian Forest Service** (created 1966); governed by the **All India Services Act, 1951**.
- **Classification:** All India Services · Central (Union) Services (e.g., IFS, IRS) · State Services.
- **Role in democracy:** a **permanent, neutral, merit-based** executive that gives continuity, policy advice, implementation and 'the steel frame' of the state.

## Administrative reforms — ARC I & II

| Commission | Year | Chair | Output |
|---|---|---|---|
| **First ARC** | 1966 | Morarji Desai (later K. Hanumanthaiya) | 20 reports (1966-70) |
| **Second ARC** | 2005 | Veerappa Moily (later V. Ramachandran) | 15 reports (2005-09) |

- 2nd ARC's first report: **'Right to Information — Master Key to Good Governance'**; others include **Ethics in Governance, Citizen Centric Administration, e-Governance (SMART)** and **Personnel Administration**.

## Andhra Pradesh administrative structure

- **State Secretariat** (Amaravati) — the political-administrative headquarters, headed by the **Chief Secretary**; organised into departments under Secretaries.
- **District administration** — after the **April 2022** reorganisation AP had **26 districts**, raised to **28** (Polavaram & Markapuram) from **31 December 2025**; each is headed by a **Collector & District Magistrate** (revenue, coordination, law & order via SP), with Revenue Divisions (RDO/Sub-Collector) and **Mandals** (Tahsildar/MRO).
- **Grama & Ward Sachivalayam system** — launched **2 October 2019**: about **15,004 village** and **3,842 ward** secretariats, staffed by functionaries and supported by **Grama/Ward Volunteers**, delivering government services at citizens' doorsteps.
keyPoints: Part XIV (Art 308-323) governs services; Art 309 (recruitment), 310 (doctrine of pleasure), 311 (dismissal safeguards), 312 (new AIS via 2/3 Rajya Sabha resolution).
Three All India Services = IAS, IPS, Indian Forest Service (1966); governed by the All India Services Act 1951.
First ARC (1966, Morarji Desai) gave 20 reports; Second ARC (2005, Veerappa Moily) gave 15 reports.
2nd ARC's first report = 'Right to Information — Master Key to Good Governance'.
AP has 28 districts (26 after the April 2022 reorganisation, 28 from 31 December 2025); Secretariat at Amaravati headed by the Chief Secretary; district headed by Collector-cum-District Magistrate.
AP Grama/Ward Sachivalayam launched 2 October 2019 — ~15,004 village and 3,842 ward secretariats with volunteers for doorstep service delivery.
items.source: Constitution of India Part XIV, Art 308-312; All India Services Act 1951; ARC-I (1966) & 2nd ARC (2005) arc.gov.in; AP reorganisation (2022) & Grama/Ward Sachivalayam Dept (2019)
